answer.label: Munger’s example — an unnamed rustic’s joke
answer.sourceLine: The reproduced 1996 Practical Thought About Practical Thought discusses a rustic who wanted to know where he would die so he would never go there. Munger presents an example rather than claiming to have invented the joke. The first-person wording on this page is a circulating recasting; this source gives the thought in third person.

author.heading: About Charlie Munger
author.bio: Charlie Munger trained as a lawyer and became Warren Buffett’s long-term investing partner at Berkshire Hathaway. He also chaired Wesco Financial and the Daily Journal Corporation. His public talks combine business examples with psychology, mathematics and lessons about practical judgment.

context.heading: The setting behind the words
lead: Munger introduces the rustic while urging listeners to consider a problem backward as well as forward. The joke illustrates avoiding a bad outcome by first identifying it. Turning that third-person illustration into first-person advice removes the story’s distinction between speaker and example. Reproduced 1996 talk ↗

schema.quotationText: You must also think in reverse, much like the rustic who wanted to know where he was going to die so that he’d never go there.

schema.claimReviewed: Charlie Munger stated the circulating first-person sentence as his own original joke: "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there"
schema.verdictNote: Munger documented this thought by retelling an unnamed rustic’s example in third person. The circulating first-person sentence recasts that example; the original joke author is unconfirmed.
schema.faqAnswer: Munger retold the rustic’s example, but the inspected 1996 text uses third person rather than this first-person sentence. That documents his use of the joke, not its original authorship.
